subject: physics

items.q: Circular ripples spread out across a ripple tank from a vibrating dipper. A student sketches a wavefront–ray diagram of the waves. Which statement correctly describes the rays on the diagram?
items.correct: They are perpendicular to the wavefronts and show the direction in which the wave's energy travels.
items.misconception: They are drawn along the crests, parallel to the wavefronts, joining points that are in phase.
items.why: Rays and wavefronts are both drawn as lines on the same diagrams, and a crest on water looks like a line the wave runs along. Examiners regularly report wavefronts and rays drawn at angles other than 90° to each other. A wavefront joins points in phase, such as a crest; the ray shows the direction in which that wavefront moves. A wavefront moves forward at right angles to itself, so the ray is perpendicular to it.
items.specStatementText: that waves travelling in two and three dimensions can be described through the concepts of wavefronts and rays
items.random_wrong: They trace the paths along which water moves outwards from the dipper as the wave travels.

items.q: A narrow beam of monochromatic light in air strikes the flat surface of a glass block along the normal, so that the angle of incidence is 0°. Which statement about what happens at the surface is correct?
items.correct: The light entering the glass keeps the frequency it had in air.
items.misconception: None of the light is reflected; it all passes into the glass.
items.why: Refraction diagrams usually show only the transmitted ray, mirrors are presented as the things that reflect, and glass is described as 'transparent'. At night you see your reflection in a window because a few per cent of the light is reflected at each glass surface while most is transmitted. The energy of the incident wave is shared between the reflected and transmitted waves.
items.specStatementText: wave behaviour at boundaries in terms of reflection, refraction and transmission
items.random_wrong: The light entering the glass changes direction as it is refracted.

items.q: A person standing behind a tree trunk about 1 m wide can clearly hear a street musician on the other side of the trunk but cannot see her. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: Sound wavelengths, roughly 0.1 m to 3 m, are comparable with the trunk's width; light's are far smaller.
items.misconception: Light travels only in straight lines and cannot diffract; only mechanical waves bend round obstacles.
items.why:
Sharp shadows and the rule 'light travels in straight lines' are taught early, while diffraction is usually demonstrated with water and sound waves. Shine a laser through a slit a fraction of a millimetre wide and the light spreads into a pattern far wider than the slit. The straight-line model works only when openings and obstacles are much larger than the wavelength.

Working: λ = v/f with v ≈ 340 m s⁻¹: sounds of about 100 Hz to 3 kHz have λ ≈ 3.4 m to 0.11 m, comparable with the 1 m trunk. Visible light has λ ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁷ m to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m, about a million times smaller than the trunk, so its diffraction is negligible.
items.specStatementText: wave diffraction around a body and through an aperture
items.random_wrong: Sound and light diffract equally round the same trunk, but the diffracted light is too dim to see.
items.working: λ = v/f with v ≈ 340 m s⁻¹: sounds of about 100 Hz to 3 kHz have λ ≈ 3.4 m to 0.11 m, comparable with the 1 m trunk. Visible light has λ ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁷ m to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m, about a million times smaller than the trunk, so its diffraction is negligible.

items.q: A wavefront diagram shows straight water waves of wavelength 2.0 cm, with wavefronts parallel to a barrier, passing through a gap 6.0 cm wide in the barrier; beyond the gap the wavefronts are straight in the middle and curved only at the edges. The gap is narrowed to 0.40 cm. How do the wavefronts beyond the gap change?
items.correct: They spread into almost semicircular wavefronts, still 2.0 cm apart.
items.misconception: They spread out less, as spreading is greatest when the gap equals λ.
items.why:
GCSE courses state that diffraction is 'most significant when the gap is the same size as the wavelength', which students read as a sharp peak at gap = λ. The rule means that diffraction becomes noticeable when the gap is comparable with λ. Narrowing the gap further makes the waves spread out even more: for gaps of about λ or less the emerging wavefronts are almost semicircular.

Working: Before: gap/λ = 6.0 cm/2.0 cm = 3, so the spreading is modest. After: gap/λ = 0.40 cm/2.0 cm = 0.20, so the waves spread into almost semicircular wavefronts. Speed and frequency are unchanged, so λ = 2.0 cm on both sides of the gap.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction
items.random_wrong: They form a narrower band of straight wavefronts, 0.40 cm wide, 2.0 cm apart.
items.working: Before: gap/λ = 6.0 cm/2.0 cm = 3, so the spreading is modest. After: gap/λ = 0.40 cm/2.0 cm = 0.20, so the waves spread into almost semicircular wavefronts. Speed and frequency are unchanged, so λ = 2.0 cm on both sides of the gap.

items.q: On a wavefront diagram, straight wavefronts in deep water make an angle of 40° with the straight boundary of a region of shallow water. The wave speed in the shallow water is 0.75 times the wave speed in the deep water. What angle do the wavefronts in the shallow water make with the boundary?
items.why:
Students know that rays and wavefronts are at 90° to each other and subtract from 90° automatically, without noticing that the boundary and the normal are also at 90°. Rotate the ray and the normal together through 90°: the ray becomes the wavefront and the normal becomes the boundary, so the angle between them is unchanged.

Working: The angle between a wavefront and the boundary equals the angle between its ray and the normal, so θ₁ = 40°. v₂/v₁ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ ⇒ sin θ₂ = 0.75 × sin 40° = 0.75 × 0.643 = 0.482 ⇒ θ₂ = 29°, which is also the angle the refracted wavefronts make with the boundary.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction
items.working: The angle between a wavefront and the boundary equals the angle between its ray and the normal, so θ₁ = 40°. v₂/v₁ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ ⇒ sin θ₂ = 0.75 × sin 40° = 0.75 × 0.643 = 0.482 ⇒ θ₂ = 29°, which is also the angle the refracted wavefronts make with the boundary.

items.q: Light meets the boundary between two transparent media. Which statement gives a condition that must be met for total internal reflection to occur?
items.correct: The light must be travelling towards a medium of lower refractive index.
items.misconception: The light must be travelling towards a medium of higher refractive index.
items.why: The word 'denser' suggests a barrier that light struggles to enter, and students remember that total internal reflection involves dense materials without remembering the direction of travel. Going from air into glass the ray bends towards the normal, so there is a refracted ray for every angle of incidence up to 90°. A critical angle exists only in the medium of higher refractive index.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law, critical angle and total internal reflection
items.random_wrong: The ray's angle to the surface must be greater than the critical angle.

items.q: A ray of light travelling in glass of refractive index 1.50 meets a flat boundary with water of refractive index 1.33. The ray makes an angle of 35.0° with the boundary. What happens to the ray at the boundary?
items.correct: It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 67.5°
items.misconception: It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 40.3°
items.why:
The surface is the line actually drawn on the diagram, and in everyday speech 'the angle at which light hits the glass' refers to the surface. Examiners regularly report angles measured from the boundary. Draw the normal first and measure every angle from it. If the angle between the ray and the surface is given, subtract it from 90°.

Working: θ₁ = 90.0° − 35.0° = 55.0°. Critical angle: sin c = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887 ⇒ c = 62.5°. θ₁ < c, so the ray is refracted (and partly reflected). n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ ⇒ sin θ₂ = (1.50 × sin 55.0°)/1.33 = (1.50 × 0.819)/1.33 = 0.924 ⇒ θ₂ = 67.5°.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law, critical angle and total internal reflection
items.random_wrong: It refracts into the water; the angle of refraction is 46.6°
items.working: θ₁ = 90.0° − 35.0° = 55.0°. Critical angle: sin c = n₂/n₁ = 1.33/1.50 = 0.887 ⇒ c = 62.5°. θ₁ < c, so the ray is refracted (and partly reflected). n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ ⇒ sin θ₂ = (1.50 × sin 55.0°)/1.33 = (1.50 × 0.819)/1.33 = 0.924 ⇒ θ₂ = 67.5°.

items.q: A ray of light passes from air into a transparent liquid. The incident ray makes an angle of 40.0° with the surface of the liquid and the refracted ray makes an angle of 55.0° with the surface. The speed of light in air is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the speed of light in the liquid?
items.why:
Sound travels faster in water and solids than in air, and students transfer this to light; 'denser' suggests more material to carry the wave. Check the ratio: in the medium with the larger n the speed and wavelength are smaller and the ray is closer to the normal. v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂.

Working: θ₁ = 90.0° − 40.0° = 50.0°; θ₂ = 90.0° − 55.0° = 35.0°. v₂/v₁ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ ⇒ v₂ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)(sin 35.0°/sin 50.0°) = (3.00 × 10⁸)(0.574/0.766) = 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law as given by n₁/n₂ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = v₂/v₁ where n is the refractive index and θ is the angle between the normal and the ray

items.q: Monochromatic light has a wavelength of 450 nm in water, of refractive index 1.33. The light passes from the water into glass of refractive index 1.50. What is its wavelength in the glass?
items.correct: 399 nm
items.misconception: 450 nm
items.why:
Students learn that 'the wave slows down' and change only that quantity, or remember that 'something stays the same' at a boundary and attach it to the wavelength instead of the frequency. Use v = fλ with f fixed: λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁. On a ripple tank the wavefronts crowd visibly closer together where the water is shallower and the waves are slower.

Working: f is unchanged ⇒ λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × (1.33/1.50) = 399 nm.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law as given by n₁/n₂ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = v₂/v₁ where n is the refractive index and θ is the angle between the normal and the ray
items.random_wrong: 508 nm
items.working: f is unchanged ⇒ λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × (1.33/1.50) = 399 nm.

items.q: Two pulses of the same shape and width travel towards each other along a stretched string. Pulse P has a maximum displacement of +3.0 cm and pulse Q a maximum displacement of −1.0 cm. Which statement about the pulses is correct?
items.correct: While their peaks coincide, the string's maximum displacement is +2.0 cm.
items.misconception: While the peaks coincide, the maximum displacement of the string is +4.0 cm.
items.why:
'Adding waves' is remembered without the sign convention, and amplitudes are always quoted as positive values. Choose upwards as positive and add with signs: +3.0 cm + (−1.0 cm) = +2.0 cm.

Working: Superposition: y = y_P + y_Q = (+3.0 cm) + (−1.0 cm) = +2.0 cm while the peaks coincide; afterwards the pulses separate with displacements +3.0 cm and −1.0 cm again.
items.specStatementText: superposition of waves and wave pulses
items.random_wrong: After they have overlapped, the pulses rebound and travel back the way they came.
items.working: Superposition: y = y_P + y_Q = (+3.0 cm) + (−1.0 cm) = +2.0 cm while the peaks coincide; afterwards the pulses separate with displacements +3.0 cm and −1.0 cm again.

items.q: Two identical sodium lamps placed side by side illuminate a white screen. No interference fringes can be seen anywhere on the screen. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: The phase difference between the light from the two lamps changes rapidly and randomly, so they are not coherent.
items.misconception: Light waves from two separate lamps cannot superpose, so they pass through each other without interfering.
items.why: Textbooks state that coherent sources are 'needed for interference', which students read as 'needed for superposition'. Superposition always happens. Coherence is what makes the interference pattern stable in position, so that it can be observed.
items.specStatementText: that double-source interference requires coherent sources
items.random_wrong: The lamps have the same frequency, so they are coherent and fringes form, but they are too fine to be seen.

items.q: Two dippers vibrating in phase act as coherent sources S₁ and S₂ on a ripple tank, producing waves of wavelength 2.0 cm. Point P is 31.0 cm from S₁ and 37.0 cm from S₂. What kind of interference occurs at P?
items.correct: Constructive: the path difference is 6.0 cm, which is 3λ
items.misconception: Destructive: the paths are 15.5λ and 18.5λ, not whole numbers of λ
items.why:
Students confuse 'path' with 'path difference', and picture each wave arriving 'at a crest' only if its own path is a whole number of wavelengths. Waves from in-phase sources arrive in phase whenever one has travelled a whole number of wavelengths farther than the other. Subtract the paths first, then compare the difference with λ.

Working: Path difference = S₂P − S₁P = 37.0 cm − 31.0 cm = 6.0 cm. 6.0 cm/2.0 cm = 3, so path difference = 3λ = nλ with n = 3 ⇒ constructive interference.
items.specStatementText: the condition for constructive interference as given by path difference = nλ
items.random_wrong: Destructive: the path difference, 3λ, is an odd number of λ
items.working: Path difference = S₂P − S₁P = 37.0 cm − 31.0 cm = 6.0 cm. 6.0 cm/2.0 cm = 3, so path difference = 3λ = nλ with n = 3 ⇒ constructive interference.

items.q: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound in phase at a frequency of 680 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the smallest path difference that gives destructive interference?
items.why:
Path difference and phase difference are introduced together, and students who have not linked them pair "one wavelength" with π, the antiphase value they meet most often; "one wavelength behind" also sounds like "out of step". Convert with phase difference = 2π × (path difference)/λ: a path difference of λ gives 2π, a whole cycle, so the waves are in phase; λ/2 gives π, antiphase. Destructive interference needs path difference = (n + ½)λ = λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, …

Working: λ = v/f = (340 m s⁻¹)/(680 Hz) = 0.50 m. Destructive: path difference = (n + ½)λ; smallest for n = 0 ⇒ 0.5 × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.working: λ = v/f = (340 m s⁻¹)/(680 Hz) = 0.50 m. Destructive: path difference = (n + ½)λ; smallest for n = 0 ⇒ 0.5 × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.

items.q: In a double-slit experiment, monochromatic light is incident normally on the slits. The amplitude at the centre of each bright fringe is twice the amplitude that one slit alone would produce there, and the amplitude at each dark fringe is zero. What has happened to the energy of the light that does not arrive at the dark fringes?
items.correct: It has been redistributed to the bright fringes, where the intensity is four times that from one slit.
items.misconception: It has been destroyed where the waves cancel, so less energy reaches the screen than passes through the slits.
items.why: 'Cancel' in everyday language means 'remove', and a zero amplitude is taken to mean the energy has vanished. At a bright fringe the amplitude is doubled, so the intensity (proportional to amplitude squared) is four times that from one slit; averaged over the pattern it is twice that from one slit, exactly as conservation of energy requires.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.random_wrong: It did not set out towards the dark fringes, which are shadows of the barrier between the two slits.

items.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic light is incident normally on two slits whose centres are 0.40 mm apart; each slit is 0.030 mm wide. The screen is 1.60 m from the slits. The distance from the centre of the 1st bright fringe to the centre of the 11th bright fringe is 24.0 mm. What is the wavelength of the light?
items.why:
A counting error (the 'fencepost' error): dividing by the number of objects rather than by the number of spaces between them. Count spaces, not fringes: from the 1st to the 11th bright fringe there are 10 fringe separations.

Working: Number of fringe separations = 11 − 1 = 10 ⇒ s = 24.0 mm/10 = 2.40 mm = 2.40 × 10⁻³ m. s = λD/d ⇒ λ = sd/D = (2.40 × 10⁻³ m)(0.40 × 10⁻³ m)/(1.60 m) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.
items.specStatementText: Young’s double-slit interference as given by s = λD/d where s is the separation of fringes, d is the separation of the slits, and D is the distance from the slits to the screen.

items.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, monochromatic red light is incident normally on the slits and the fringe separation on the screen is 2.0 mm. Which single change would make the fringe separation 4.0 mm?
items.correct: Halving the distance between the centres of the two slits
items.misconception: Doubling the distance between the centres of the slits
items.why:
It seems natural that spreading out the sources spreads out the pattern, and s and d are both called 'separations', suggesting they change together. With a larger d, the path difference changes more quickly with angle, so successive maxima occur at smaller angles: s is proportional to 1/d.

Working: s = λD/d ⇒ s ∝ 1/d. Halving d: s = 2 × 2.0 mm = 4.0 mm.
items.specStatementText: Young’s double-slit interference as given by s = λD/d where s is the separation of fringes, d is the separation of the slits, and D is the distance from the slits to the screen.
items.random_wrong: Using blue light, of shorter wavelength, in place of the red
items.working: s = λD/d ⇒ s ∝ 1/d. Halving d: s = 2 × 2.0 mm = 4.0 mm.

items.q: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a single rectangular slit of width 0.12 mm. A screen is 2.0 m from the slit. What is the width of the central maximum on the screen, measured between the first minima on either side?
items.why:
The width of the central maximum is the feature students picture, and the equation is remembered without its diagram. Missing factors of 2 in single-slit calculations are a recurring comment in examiner reports. Sketch the pattern and mark θ from the centre line. The width on a screen is about 2Dθ = 2λD/b.

Working: θ = λ/b = (600 × 10⁻⁹ m)/(0.12 × 10⁻³ m) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ rad (centre to first minimum). Width = 2Dθ = 2 × 2.0 m × 5.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10⁻² m.
items.specStatementText: single-slit diffraction including intensity patterns as given by θ = λ/b where b is the slit width
items.working: θ = λ/b = (600 × 10⁻⁹ m)/(0.12 × 10⁻³ m) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ rad (centre to first minimum). Width = 2Dθ = 2 × 2.0 m × 5.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10⁻² m.

items.q: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a single slit, and the diffraction pattern is viewed on a distant screen. The slit width is then reduced from 0.20 mm to 0.10 mm. How does the central maximum change?
items.correct: It becomes twice as wide and less intense, as less light passes and is spread over a wider angle.
items.misconception: It becomes half as wide and less intense, as it is an image of a slit that is now half as wide.
items.why: It extends the trimmed-beam model (m10) from the beam to the intensity pattern: straight-line (geometric) optics predicts a bright patch the size of the slit. Ambrose and colleagues found university students applying this geometric model to narrow slits. For slits only a few hundred wavelengths wide or less, the pattern is set by diffraction, not geometry: with λ = 600 nm, b = 0.10 mm and D = 2.0 m the central maximum is about 2λD/b = 24 mm wide, 240 times the slit width. Halving b doubles this width.
items.specStatementText: single-slit diffraction including intensity patterns as given by θ = λ/b where b is the slit width
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged, as both slits are far wider than 600 nm, so neither diffracts significantly.

items.q: Monochromatic light is incident normally on two slits, each of width b, whose centres are a distance d apart, where d is several times b. Which describes the pattern on a distant screen?
items.correct: Equally spaced fringes whose brightness follows the single-slit pattern, fading at its minima
items.misconception: Equally spaced fringes of equal brightness across the whole screen, as in the ideal Young's pattern
items.why: The ideal Young's pattern, derived for very narrow slits, is drawn with fringes of equal brightness, and s = λD/d says nothing about intensity. Each slit sends light mainly into its own single-slit pattern. Where that pattern is zero, neither slit sends any light, so no fringe can form there.
items.specStatementText: that the single-slit pattern modulates the double slit interference pattern
items.random_wrong: Fringes whose spacing is set by the slit width b, within an envelope whose width is set by d alone

items.q: A double slit has slits of width b = 0.10 mm whose centres are d = 0.30 mm apart. It is illuminated normally with monochromatic light. How many bright interference fringes lie within the central maximum of the single-slit diffraction envelope?
items.why:
θ = λ/b and s = λD/d have the same form and both refer to 'slits', so the roles of the two lengths are easily swapped. Since b is smaller than d, the envelope (λ/b) is wider than the fringe spacing (λ/d), so several fringes fit inside its central maximum.

Working: Interference maxima: sin θ = nλ/d. First envelope minimum: sin θ = λ/b. Fringes inside the central maximum satisfy n < d/b = 0.30 mm/0.10 mm = 3, so n = 0, ±1, ±2 (n = ±3 coincides with the minima and is missing): 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 fringes.
items.specStatementText: that the single-slit pattern modulates the double slit interference pattern
items.working: Interference maxima: sin θ = nλ/d. First envelope minimum: sin θ = λ/b. Fringes inside the central maximum satisfy n < d/b = 0.30 mm/0.10 mm = 3, so n = 0, ±1, ±2 (n = ±3 coincides with the minima and is missing): 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 fringes.

items.q: Light of wavelength 650 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating that has 600 lines per millimetre. At what angle to the straight-through direction is the second-order maximum observed?
items.why:
Counting the bright lines from the centre naturally starts at 1. Label maxima by path difference: at the central maximum the path difference is zero, so n = 0.

Working: d = 1/(600 mm⁻¹) = 1/(6.00 × 10⁵ m⁻¹) = 1.667 × 10⁻⁶ m. nλ = d sin θ ⇒ sin θ = 2 × 650 × 10⁻⁹ m × 6.00 × 10⁵ m⁻¹ = 0.780 ⇒ θ = 51.3°.
items.specStatementText: interference patterns from multiple slits and diffraction gratings as given by nλ = d sin θ.

items.q: Monochromatic light is incident normally first on a double slit and then on a diffraction grating whose adjacent slits have the same separation d as the double slit. Every slit is equally illuminated. Compared with the double-slit fringes, how do the grating's principal maxima appear?
items.correct: At the same angles as the double-slit fringes, but much sharper and brighter
items.misconception: Farther apart than the fringes, because the grating has many more slits
items.why: Gratings are described by 'lines per millimetre': more lines per millimetre means a smaller d and more widely spread maxima, and students confuse this with simply having more lines. Keep the two ideas apart: the spacing d fixes the angles; the number of slits fixes how sharp and bright the maxima are.
items.specStatementText: interference patterns from multiple slits and diffraction gratings as given by nλ = d sin θ.
items.random_wrong: At the same angles, but wider and dimmer, as the light is shared among more slits

items.q: White light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. Which describes the pattern seen on a screen?
items.correct: A white central maximum, with a spectrum in each order on either side and violet nearest the centre
items.misconception: A white central maximum, with a spectrum in each order on either side and red nearest the centre
items.why: The prism spectrum is met first, and its colour order is transferred to diffraction without checking the equation. Read the order from nλ = d sin θ (or s = λD/d): the longer the wavelength, the larger the angle. Refraction and diffraction separate colours by different mechanisms and in opposite orders.
items.specStatementText: interference patterns from multiple slits and diffraction gratings as given by nλ = d sin θ.
items.random_wrong: A spectrum at the centre, as well as in each order on either side, with violet nearest to the centre

items.q: Light containing just two wavelengths, 450 nm and 700 nm, is incident normally on a diffraction grating with slit spacing d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m. Which statement about the maxima produced is correct?
items.correct: On each side, the 450 nm light gives maxima up to order 4, but the 700 nm light only up to order 2.
items.misconception: On each side, the 450 nm light gives maxima up to order 4, and the 700 nm light up to order 3.
items.why:
Habitual rounding to the nearest integer, without checking the physical limit sin θ ≤ 1. For d/λ = 2.86, the order n = 3 would need sin θ = 1.05, which is impossible, so the highest order is 2.

Working: n_max = largest whole number ≤ d/λ. 450 nm: d/λ = (2.00 × 10⁻⁶)/(450 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.44 ⇒ n_max = 4. 700 nm: d/λ = (2.00 × 10⁻⁶)/(700 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.86 ⇒ n_max = 2 (n = 3 would need sin θ = 1.05).
items.specStatementText: interference patterns from multiple slits and diffraction gratings as given by nλ = d sin θ.
items.random_wrong: The 700 nm light gives more orders than the 450 nm light, because red light is deviated less.
items.working: n_max = largest whole number ≤ d/λ. 450 nm: d/λ = (2.00 × 10⁻⁶)/(450 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.44 ⇒ n_max = 4. 700 nm: d/λ = (2.00 × 10⁻⁶)/(700 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.86 ⇒ n_max = 2 (n = 3 would need sin θ = 1.05).

items.q: A small loudspeaker in open air emits sound of frequency 170 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. A student draws a wavefront–ray diagram of the sound in a horizontal plane through the speaker. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
items.correct: Adjacent wavefronts are 2.0 m apart, both close to the speaker and far from it.
items.misconception: Every compression and every rarefaction has a wavefront, so neighbouring ones are 1.0 m apart.
items.why:
Many textbook diagrams draw crests as solid lines and troughs as dashed lines between them, so adjacent drawn lines really are λ/2 apart, and students transfer this spacing to diagrams that show crests only. The same confusion appears when students measure a wavelength from a crest to the next trough. Check what the lines represent. If every line is a crest (all points in phase), adjacent lines are one wavelength apart. Only when troughs are drawn as well is the spacing between neighbouring lines λ/2.

Working: λ = v/f = 340 m s⁻¹ / 170 Hz = 2.0 m. Wavefronts are drawn through points in phase (successive compressions), so adjacent wavefronts are λ = 2.0 m apart, and this spacing is the same at every distance from the speaker because v and f are unchanged. The wavefronts are circles (sections of spheres) centred on the speaker; rays are radial, perpendicular to them.
items.specStatementText: that waves travelling in two and three dimensions can be described through the concepts of wavefronts and rays
items.random_wrong: The rays show the paths along which air is carried outward from the speaker.
items.working: λ = v/f = 340 m s⁻¹ / 170 Hz = 2.0 m. Wavefronts are drawn through points in phase (successive compressions), so adjacent wavefronts are λ = 2.0 m apart, and this spacing is the same at every distance from the speaker because v and f are unchanged. The wavefronts are circles (sections of spheres) centred on the speaker; rays are radial, perpendicular to them.

items.q: Straight water waves of frequency 5.0 Hz travel at 0.40 m s⁻¹ across the deep part of a ripple tank towards a boundary with a shallow region, in which the wave speed is 0.20 m s⁻¹. The wavefronts are parallel to the boundary. Which statement about the waves at the boundary is correct?
items.correct: The reflected waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm and the transmitted waves 4.0 cm.
items.misconception: The transmitted waves have a frequency of 2.5 Hz, half that of the incident waves.
items.why:
Speed and frequency are both described in everyday language as how 'fast' a wave is, and v = fλ is remembered without asking which quantity the boundary can change. Students also see wavefronts closer together in the slower medium and read the closer spacing as a change in frequency. Each wavefront that arrives at the boundary produces one wavefront on the other side, so the number of wavefronts per second, the frequency, cannot change. Apply v = fλ with f fixed: halving the speed halves the wavelength.

Working: Incident wavelength λ₁ = v₁/f = 0.40/5.0 = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm. The reflected wave travels back in the deep water at 0.40 m s⁻¹ with the same frequency, so its wavelength is also 8.0 cm. The transmitted wave keeps f = 5.0 Hz, so λ₂ = v₂/f = 0.20/5.0 = 0.040 m = 4.0 cm. Part of the wave is reflected and part transmitted, even at normal incidence.
items.specStatementText: wave behaviour at boundaries in terms of reflection, refraction and transmission
items.random_wrong: The transmitted waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm, the same as that of the incident waves.
items.working: Incident wavelength λ₁ = v₁/f = 0.40/5.0 = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm. The reflected wave travels back in the deep water at 0.40 m s⁻¹ with the same frequency, so its wavelength is also 8.0 cm. The transmitted wave keeps f = 5.0 Hz, so λ₂ = v₂/f = 0.20/5.0 = 0.040 m = 4.0 cm. Part of the wave is reflected and part transmitted, even at normal incidence.

items.q: Two radio stations broadcast from the same mast: station A at 1.0 MHz, wavelength 300 m, and station B at 100 MHz, wavelength 3.0 m. A house stands in a valley behind a hill about 200 m high, with no straight-line path from the mast to the house. Which station is more likely to be received at the house, and why?
items.correct: Station A, because its 300 m wavelength is comparable with the hill's size, so it diffracts round it.
items.misconception: Station B, because its 100 MHz waves carry more energy and so pass over the hill more easily.
items.why:
GCSE courses teach that higher-frequency electromagnetic waves (X-rays, gamma rays) are more energetic and more penetrating, and students extend 'more penetrating' to mean 'better at getting round hills and buildings'. Penetration through a material and diffraction around an obstacle are different things. For diffraction the only comparison that matters is wavelength against obstacle size: the longer the wavelength, the more the wave spreads into the region behind the obstacle.

Working: Diffraction around a body is significant when λ is comparable with or larger than the body. Station A: λ = 300 m, of the same order as the 200 m hill, so the waves spread strongly into the valley behind it. Station B: λ = 3.0 m, about 70 times smaller than the hill, so it diffracts very little and the hill shadows the house. Station A is the one more likely to be received.
items.specStatementText: wave diffraction around a body and through an aperture
items.random_wrong: Both equally, because the hill is the same size for both, and it alone fixes how much a wave diffracts.
items.working: Diffraction around a body is significant when λ is comparable with or larger than the body. Station A: λ = 300 m, of the same order as the 200 m hill, so the waves spread strongly into the valley behind it. Station B: λ = 3.0 m, about 70 times smaller than the hill, so it diffracts very little and the hill shadows the house. Station A is the one more likely to be received.

items.q: Two pulses of identical shape and size but opposite displacement travel towards each other along a stretched string. At one instant they overlap exactly and the whole string is momentarily straight. Which statement about this instant, and what follows it, is correct?
items.correct: The string is straight but moving; the pulses then emerge and continue past each other.
items.misconception: The pulses have cancelled each other out; the string stays straight from now on.
items.why: Students picture the instant of overlap as the final state, as when two blobs of clay join. Research on pulses (Wittmann and colleagues) found students describing overlapping pulses as combining or destroying each other. Each pulse carries its own energy along the string in its own direction; superposition describes the displacement only during the overlap.
items.specStatementText: superposition of waves and wave pulses
items.random_wrong: The string is straight and at rest; the pulses' energy has become internal energy of the string.

items.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment using a filament lamp, the light passes through a single narrow slit before it reaches the double slit. What is the purpose of the single slit?
items.correct: It lights both slits with the same wavefronts, so the two slits act as coherent sources.
items.misconception: It makes the light monochromatic, because sources of a single frequency are automatically coherent.
items.why: Coherence is often defined as 'the same frequency and a constant phase difference', and students remember only the first part; 'monochromatic' is taken to mean 'coherent'. A lamp emits light from many atoms in short, random bursts, so the phase of its light jumps randomly. Two lamps with identical frequencies still have a randomly changing phase difference.
items.specStatementText: that double-source interference requires coherent sources
items.random_wrong: It turns the lamp's light into laser-like light, without which stable fringes cannot be produced.

items.q: Two loudspeakers, driven in phase by the same signal generator, face a line along which a microphone is moved. Starting from the central maximum of loudness, the microphone is moved along the line to the third maximum away from the centre. At that point its distances from the two speakers differ by 0.60 m. What is the wavelength of the sound?
items.why:
Half-wavelengths appear in several nearby results (node spacing on a standing wave is λ/2, and the destructive condition involves ½λ), so 'multiples of λ/2' is remembered as the general condition for anything to do with interference. Picture the two waves arriving: a path difference of a whole wavelength brings crest onto crest (constructive); an extra half-wavelength brings crest onto trough (destructive). Write the two conditions side by side, nλ and (n + ½)λ, and test with n = 1.

Working: Sources in phase: maxima where the path difference is nλ, with n = 0 at the central maximum. The third maximum away from the centre has n = 3, so 3λ = 0.60 m and λ = 0.20 m.
items.specStatementText: the condition for constructive interference as given by path difference = nλ
items.working: Sources in phase: maxima where the path difference is nλ, with n = 0 at the central maximum. The third maximum away from the centre has n = 3, so 3λ = 0.60 m and λ = 0.20 m.

items.q: The diagram shows straight water waves in a ripple tank crossing the boundary between region X and region Y. The wavefronts, a ray and the normal at the point where the ray crosses the boundary are drawn. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The waves travel more slowly in Y, so Y is the shallower water.
items.misconception: The waves travel more slowly in Y, so Y is the deeper water.
items.why: Breaking waves near a beach grow taller and look as if they are rushing in, and everyday language speaks of waves 'racing up the sand'. The taller, steeper waves are read as faster ones, whereas they are in fact slowing down. In a ripple tank, waves crossing from deep to shallow water have their wavefronts closer together on the shallow side: the same frequency with a shorter wavelength means a lower speed. Shallow water always slows the wave.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction
items.random_wrong: The waves travel faster in Y, as the ray bends towards the normal there.

items.q: A student's sketch of water waves passing through a gap in a barrier is shown. The sketch is drawn to the scale marked, and the water is of the same depth everywhere. Which feature of the sketch is incorrect?
items.correct: The wavefronts beyond the gap are drawn closer together than those approaching it.
items.misconception: The wavefronts beyond the gap are drawn curved instead of as a straight beam.
items.why: Light through large openings, such as a torch beam through a doorway, seems simply to be trimmed by the gap. Ambrose and colleagues found students apply this geometric (ray) model to narrow slits. Every point on a wavefront in the gap acts as a source of secondary wavelets; the fewer wavelengths fit across the gap, the more the emerging wave spreads.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction
items.random_wrong: The rays beyond the gap are drawn at right angles to the wavefronts, not along them.

items.q: The diagram shows a ray of light inside a semicircular glass block of refractive index 1.50, surrounded by air of refractive index 1.00. The ray travels along a radius to the centre C of the flat face, making the angle marked with the flat face. What happens to the ray at C?
items.correct: It refracts into the air, leaving at 59.4° to the normal.
items.misconception: It refracts into the air, emerging at 35.0° to the normal.
items.why:
Most practice problems start in air (n₁ = 1.00), so students learn λ₂ = λ₁/n₂ and sin θ₂ = sin θ₁/n₂ instead of the general form. Use n₁/n₂ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = v₂/v₁ = λ₂/λ₁ with both refractive indices every time.

Working: The angle marked, 55°, is between the ray and the flat face, so the angle of incidence (from the normal) is θ₁ = 90° − 55° = 35°. Critical angle for glass to air: sin c = 1.00/1.50 ⇒ c = 41.8°. Since 35° < 41.8°, the ray refracts into the air (with some partial reflection): 1.50 sin 35° = 1.00 sin θ₂ ⇒ sin θ₂ = 0.860 ⇒ θ₂ = 59.4°. The ray enters the curved face along a radius, so it is undeviated there.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law, critical angle and total internal reflection
items.random_wrong: It refracts into the air at 22.5° to the normal.
items.working: The angle marked, 55°, is between the ray and the flat face, so the angle of incidence (from the normal) is θ₁ = 90° − 55° = 35°. items.q: The graph shows the displacement y of a stretched string against position x at time t = 0. Pulse A is travelling to the right and pulse B to the left, each at a speed of 1.0 cm s⁻¹. What is the displacement of the string at x = 6.0 cm when t = 3.0 s?
items.correct: 0.5 cm
items.misconception: 2.0 cm
items.why:
Amplitude and displacement are easily conflated, and the worked examples students meet usually show two peaks coinciding, where adding the amplitudes happens to give the right answer. Read each pulse's displacement at the point and time in question, with its sign, and add those two values. Sketch each pulse in its new position first; the amplitude only enters where the point lies at a peak.

Working: At t = 0, A is a triangle from x = 2 to 6 cm with its peak of +3.0 cm at x = 4 cm; B is a triangle from x = 8 to 10 cm with its trough of −1.0 cm at x = 9 cm. In 3.0 s each pulse moves 3.0 cm. At t = 3.0 s, A spans x = 5 to 9 cm with its peak at x = 7 cm: at x = 6 cm it is halfway up the leading edge, displacement +3.0 × (1/2) = +1.5 cm. B spans x = 5 to 7 cm with its trough at x = 6 cm: displacement −1.0 cm. Superposition: y = +1.5 + (−1.0) = +0.5 cm.
items.specStatementText: superposition of waves and wave pulses
items.random_wrong: 2.5 cm

items.q: The diagram shows two point sources S₁ and S₂ in a ripple tank, vibrating in phase, and a point P on the water surface. The waves have a wavelength of 2.0 cm. On which line of the interference pattern does P lie?
items.correct: On the first maximum to one side of the central maximum.
items.misconception: On no maximum, because P is not equidistant from S₁ and S₂.
items.why:
'In phase' is read as 'having travelled the same distance', and diagrams highlight the central maximum. A path difference of λ, 2λ, … delays one wave by whole cycles, which leaves the two waves in phase. Each value of n gives its own line of maxima.

Working: S₁P = 15.0 cm and S₁S₂ = 8.0 cm meet at a right angle at S₁, so S₂P = √(15.0² + 8.0²) = √289 = 17.0 cm. Path difference = 17.0 − 15.0 = 2.0 cm = 1 × λ, a whole number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in phase: constructive interference (n = 1).
items.specStatementText: the condition for constructive interference as given by path difference = nλ
items.random_wrong: On the first minimum to one side of the central maximum line.

items.q: The graph shows how the intensity I of the light on a screen varies with position x in a Young's double-slit experiment. The two slits are 0.40 mm apart and each is 0.020 mm wide; the screen is 2.0 m from the slits, and monochromatic light is incident normally on them. What is the wavelength of the light?
items.why:
Both are small slit dimensions quoted in millimetres, and 'slit width' and 'slit separation' are easily confused when both appear in a question. Label a sketch: b is across one slit; d runs from the centre of one slit to the centre of the other. Only d appears in s = λD/d.

Working: From the graph, adjacent maxima are at x = 0, 3, 6 mm, so the fringe separation is s = 3.0 mm = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m. s = λD/d ⇒ λ = sd/D = (3.0 × 10⁻³ m × 0.40 × 10⁻³ m)/2.0 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (600 nm).

items.q: The graph shows the intensity pattern produced on a distant screen when monochromatic light is incident normally on two rectangular slits of width b whose centres are a distance d apart. The dashed line is the single-slit diffraction envelope. What is the value of the ratio d/b?
items.why:
The width of the central maximum is the feature students picture, and the equation is remembered without its diagram. Missing factors of 2 in single-slit calculations are a recurring comment in examiner reports. Sketch the pattern and mark θ from the centre line. The width on a screen is about 2Dθ = 2λD/b.

Working: Interference maxima occur at sin θ ≈ θ = nλ/d; the single-slit envelope has its first minimum at θ = λ/b. On the graph the envelope falls to zero exactly where the 4th-order fringe would be (the central lobe holds orders 0, ±1, ±2, ±3 and the ±4 fringes are missing), so 4λ/d = λ/b, giving d/b = 4.
items.specStatementText: that the single-slit pattern modulates the double slit interference pattern

items.q: Is a ray a physical part of a wave, such as a thin beam of light?
items.correct: No. A ray is a line drawn to show the direction in which the wave's energy travels. The wave fills the whole region, including the spaces between the rays that happen to be drawn.
items.misconception: Rays are physical beams that make up the wave, so there is no wave between the rays drawn on a diagram.
items.why: Ray diagrams show only a few lines, and laser beams and sunbeams through gaps look like 'rays'. Research on students' understanding of geometrical optics (Goldberg and McDermott) found that many students treat the rays drawn on a diagram as the only light present. Treat rays as arrows on a map of the wave: at each point they are perpendicular to the wavefronts and show the direction of energy flow. Any number of rays could be drawn; the wave itself is continuous.
items.specStatementText: that waves travelling in two and three dimensions can be described through the concepts of wavefronts and rays
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a ray show the path along which the medium moves away from the source?
items.correct: No. A wave transfers energy, not matter. The particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions; the ray shows the direction in which the energy travels.
items.misconception: Waves carry the medium along with them, so a ray traces the path of particles travelling outwards from the source.
items.why: Breaking waves on a beach and objects swept along by currents suggest that water travels with a wave, and the word 'travel' is used for both waves and objects. A cork floating on a ripple tank bobs up and down as the waves pass but does not move outwards with them. Only the disturbance and its energy move along the ray.
items.specStatementText: that waves travelling in two and three dimensions can be described through the concepts of wavefronts and rays

items.q: Does light always change direction when it enters a different medium?
items.correct: No. Along the normal (normal incidence) the speed and wavelength change but the direction does not.
items.misconception: Refraction means bending, so light always changes direction on entering a different medium, even when it travels along the normal.
items.why: Refraction is introduced as 'the bending of light', and almost every diagram shows an oblique ray, so the change of direction is taken to be the whole of refraction. Refraction is caused by the change of speed; the direction changes only when the wave meets the boundary obliquely. With θ₁ = 0, Snell's law gives sin θ₂ = 0, so a ray along the normal stays on the normal.
items.specStatementText: wave behaviour at boundaries in terms of reflection, refraction and transmission
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the amount of diffraction depend only on the size of the gap or obstacle?
items.correct: No. It depends on the size of the gap or obstacle compared with the wavelength.
items.misconception: Diffraction depends only on the size of the gap or obstacle, so all waves meeting the same obstacle diffract by the same amount.
items.why: Rules such as 'a narrower gap gives more diffraction' are first learned with a single type of wave of fixed wavelength (ripple-tank waves), so the wavelength drops out of the rule. Always compare the wavelength with the size. The same 1 m wide doorway diffracts sound of wavelength about 1 m strongly and light of wavelength about 5 × 10⁻⁷ m negligibly.
items.specStatementText: wave diffraction around a body and through an aperture
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does diffraction change the wavelength of a wave?
items.correct: No. The wave stays in the same medium, with the same speed and frequency, so its wavelength is unchanged.
items.misconception: Waves that squeeze through a gap have their wavelength changed, usually shortened, as they pass through.
items.why: Diffracted wavefronts are often drawn freehand with uneven spacing, and diffraction is confused with refraction, where the wavelength does change. Only the shape of the wavefronts changes. On a correct diagram, the wavefronts beyond the gap are the same distance apart as those before it.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a wave slows down on crossing a boundary obliquely, which way does it bend?
items.correct: Towards the normal. A wave that speeds up bends away from the normal.
items.misconception: A wave that slows down bends away from the normal, and one that speeds up bends towards it.
items.why: The rule is memorised as a pair of phrases whose directions are easily swapped, and the picture of a denser medium 'pushing the wave back' reinforces the reversed version. Follow a wavefront: the end that enters the slow medium first travels less far in the same time, so the wavefront pivots and the ray turns towards the normal. Snell's law agrees: v₂ < v₁ gives sin θ₂ < sin θ₁.
items.specStatementText: wavefront-ray diagrams showing refraction and diffraction

items.q: Is the critical angle always given by sin c = 1/n?
items.correct: No. sin c = n₂/n₁; sin c = 1/n is the special case in which the second medium is air (n₂ = 1.00).
items.misconception: The critical angle is a fixed property of a material, given by sin c = 1/n whatever medium is on the other side of the boundary.
items.why: Almost all introductory examples use glass–air or water–air boundaries, where n₂ = 1.00 disappears from the formula. Derive it from Snell's law with θ₂ = 90°: n₁ sin c = n₂. A glass–water boundary (1.50 to 1.33) has c = 62.5°, much larger than the glass–air value of 41.8°.

items.q: Does total internal reflection happen when the angle of incidence equals the critical angle?
items.correct: No. At exactly the critical angle the refracted ray just grazes along the boundary; total internal reflection needs an angle of incidence greater than c.
items.misconception: Total internal reflection happens when the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle.
items.why: The critical angle is introduced through the special diagram in which the refracted ray runs along the surface, so students remember 'the critical angle' as the condition for total internal reflection itself. State both conditions in full: the light travels towards a lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence is greater than c.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law, critical angle and total internal reflection

items.q: Can the sines in Snell's law be cancelled so that the angles are in the ratio of the speeds?
items.correct: No. sin θ₂/sin θ₁ is not equal to θ₂/θ₁; sine is a function of the angle, not a factor.
items.misconception: sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = θ₂/θ₁, so the angles themselves are in the same ratio as the speeds.
items.why: An algebraic slip: 'sin' is treated as a multiplying factor that cancels from top and bottom. The small-angle approximation, in which sin θ ≈ θ, makes this look acceptable. Evaluate each sine separately. For 35° and 50° the ratio of the sines is 0.749, noticeably different from the ratio of the angles, 0.700.
items.specStatementText: Snell’s law as given by n₁/n₂ = sin θ₂/sin θ₁ = v₂/v₁ where n is the refractive index and θ is the angle between the normal and the ray
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to two pulses when they meet on a string?
items.correct: They pass through each other. While they overlap their displacements add; afterwards each continues with its original shape and direction.
items.misconception: Pulses collide and bounce off each other like balls, returning the way they came.
items.why: Students apply a particle model to pulses, drawing on experience of colliding objects. Wittmann, Steinberg and Redish documented this particle-like reasoning about waves and pulses. Pulses are disturbances of the medium, not objects. Superposition gives the displacement while they overlap, and then they pass through each other unchanged.
items.specStatementText: superposition of waves and wave pulses

items.q: Is a laser needed to produce interference fringes with light?
items.correct: No. Any light can be used if it is divided from one source so that the two parts are coherent, as in Young's own experiment with sunlight passed through a small hole.
items.misconception: Stable interference of light can be produced only with laser light.
items.why: School demonstrations of double-slit interference almost always use a laser, because its light is bright and coherent across the whole beam. A lamp behind a single narrow slit, followed by a double slit, gives visible fringes: both slits are lit by the same wavefronts, so they act as coherent sources.
items.specStatementText: that double-source interference requires coherent sources

items.q: Does a path difference of an odd number of whole wavelengths give destructive interference?
items.correct: No. Any whole number of wavelengths, odd or even, gives constructive interference. Destructive interference needs an odd number of half-wavelengths, (n + ½)λ.
items.misconception: A path difference of an odd number of wavelengths (3λ, 5λ, …) gives destructive interference.
items.why: The destructive condition is often worded as 'an odd multiple of half a wavelength'; students remember 'odd multiple' and drop 'half'. Count in half-wavelengths: 3λ is six half-wavelengths, an even number, so the waves arrive in phase.
items.specStatementText: the condition for constructive interference as given by path difference = nλ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the smallest value of n in path difference = (n + ½)λ?
items.correct: n = 0, which gives the smallest path difference for destructive interference, λ/2.
items.misconception: n starts at 1, so the smallest path difference for destructive interference is 1½λ.
items.why: Counting usually starts at 1, and the phrase 'first minimum' suggests n = 1. n = 0, 1, 2, … . The minimum nearest the centre has n = 0 and a path difference of λ/2.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the wavelength found from the wave speed and the frequency?
items.correct: λ = v/f.
items.misconception: λ = f/v, the wave equation rearranged the wrong way up.
items.why: A rearrangement slip in v = fλ that goes unnoticed when the units are not checked: f/v has the unit s⁻¹/(m s⁻¹) = m⁻¹, not a length. Divide both sides of v = fλ by f. Check the unit: (m s⁻¹)/(s⁻¹) = m.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are bright fringes images of the slits and dark fringes shadows of the barrier?
items.correct: No. The fringes are an interference pattern: light from both slits reaches every point, and the dark fringes are where it arrives in antiphase.
items.misconception: Bright fringes are images of the slits formed by light travelling straight through them, and the dark regions are shadows of the solid parts of the barrier.
items.why: Students apply the straight-line (geometric) model of light. Ambrose, Shaffer, Steinberg and McDermott found this 'image of the slits' reasoning widespread among university physics students. There are many more fringes than slits, and their spacing depends on the wavelength. Covering one slit makes the dark fringes light up: they were dark only because the light from the two slits cancelled there.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At a dark fringe, is the energy of the light converted into thermal energy?
items.correct: No. Almost no energy arrives at a dark fringe; it is redistributed to the bright fringes.
items.misconception: When waves cancel, their energy is converted into internal (thermal) energy at that place.
items.why: Students know energy must be conserved and reach for the standard answer for 'missing' energy from earlier courses: that it has been 'lost as heat'. Heating at a point needs energy to be delivered and absorbed there, and a zero amplitude means no energy is arriving. The energy flow is steered towards the bright fringes.
items.specStatementText: the condition for destructive interference as given by path difference = (n + ½)λ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can lengths given in millimetres be substituted directly into s = λD/d?
items.correct: No. Every length must be in metres (or all in the same unit) before it is substituted.
items.misconception: Small lengths quoted in millimetres can be substituted as given, alongside other quantities in metres.
items.why: Slit widths and separations are quoted in mm; the number is copied and the factor of 10⁻³ is forgotten, a procedural error regularly noted in examiner reports. Convert first: 0.40 mm = 0.40 × 10⁻³ m. Then check the size of the answer: a visible wavelength is a few times 10⁻⁷ m. The same applies to b in θ = λ/b.
items.specStatementText: Young’s double-slit interference as given by s = λD/d where s is the separation of fringes, d is the separation of the slits, and D is the distance from the slits to the screen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does light of shorter wavelength give more widely spaced double-slit fringes?
items.correct: No. s = λD/d, so a shorter wavelength gives fringes closer together.
items.misconception: Shorter-wavelength (bluer) light spreads out more, as violet does in a prism, so it gives wider fringe spacing.
items.why: The prism spectrum, in which violet is deviated most, is met first and its colour order is carried over to interference. Read it from s = λD/d: s is proportional to λ, so red fringes are more widely spaced than blue ones.
items.specStatementText: Young’s double-slit interference as given by s = λD/d where s is the separation of fringes, d is the separation of the slits, and D is the distance from the slits to the screen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the angle given by θ = λ/b in degrees?
items.correct: No. θ = λ/b is a small-angle result, and the angle it gives is in radians.
items.misconception: The angle given by θ = λ/b is in degrees.
items.why: Calculators default to degrees, and other angles in this topic (in Snell's law and in nλ = d sin θ) are usually quoted in degrees. λ/b is a ratio of two lengths, which is an angle in radians. Use it directly (arc length ≈ Dθ) or convert with 1 rad = 57.3°.
items.specStatementText: single-slit diffraction including intensity patterns as given by θ = λ/b where b is the slit width
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the intensity of the central maximum depend on the slit width?
items.correct: Yes. A narrower slit lets less light through and spreads it over a wider angle, so the central maximum is less intense.
items.misconception: The brightness of the central maximum depends only on the light source; changing the slit width changes only how far the pattern spreads.
items.why: Intensity graphs in textbooks are usually normalised, with the central peak drawn at the same height whatever the slit width, and earlier courses discuss only the spreading. Less light passes through a narrower slit, and it is spread over a larger angle, so the central maximum is dimmer. The guide requires this effect of slit width on intensity to be considered qualitatively.
items.specStatementText: single-slit diffraction including intensity patterns as given by θ = λ/b where b is the slit width
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can grating angles be found from θ = nλ/d in radians?
items.correct: No. Grating angles are often large, so sin θ = nλ/d must be used; θ ≈ nλ/d holds only for small angles.
items.misconception: The small-angle forms used for single and double slits apply to gratings as well, so θ = nλ/d in radians.
items.why: θ = λ/b and s = λD/d, both small-angle results, are met first and carried over without noticing that grating angles can be tens of degrees. Use sin θ = nλ/d. For sin θ = 0.78, θ = 51.3°, whereas 0.78 rad is only 44.7°.
items.specStatementText: interference patterns from multiple slits and diffraction gratings as given by nλ = d sin θ.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: For a grating with 600 lines per millimetre, is d = 1/600 m?
items.misconception: The grating spacing is 1/N in metres, whatever unit of length the number of lines N is quoted per.
items.why: Taking the reciprocal of N is remembered, but the 'per millimetre' is lost in the process. Convert N first: 600 lines per mm = 6.00 × 10⁵ lines per metre, so d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m. A spacing of millimetres would give angles far too small to observe.

items.q: Does sharing light among more slits make the maxima dimmer and wider?
items.correct: No. With each slit equally illuminated, more slits pass more light, and it is concentrated into narrower, brighter maxima.
items.misconception: With more slits the light is shared among them, so each maximum becomes dimmer and more spread out.
items.why: Everyday 'sharing' reasoning, and the single-slit result that a narrower opening gives a dimmer pattern, are transferred to the number of slits. Waves from many slits reinforce only at the angles given by nλ = d sin θ; slightly away from those angles they cancel. More slits make that cancellation sharper and put more light into each maximum.

items.q: Does the grating pattern depend only on d and λ, since the number of slits is not in nλ = d sin θ?
items.correct: Only the positions of the maxima do. Their sharpness and brightness depend on the number of slits illuminated.
items.misconception: If the number of slits does not appear in nλ = d sin θ, it has no effect on the pattern at all.
items.why: Students judge what matters by what appears in the equation, forgetting that the equation gives only the positions of the maxima. nλ = d sin θ locates the maxima; it says nothing about their width or intensity, which improve as more slits are used.

items.q: Is the central maximum of a white-light grating pattern a spectrum?
items.correct: No. At n = 0 the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours coincide and the central maximum is white.
items.misconception: A grating splits white light into colours at every maximum, including the central one.
items.why: 'A grating splits light into a spectrum' is remembered as a general rule, and a prism disperses all the light that passes through it. Put n = 0 into nλ = d sin θ: θ = 0 for every wavelength. Colours separate only in the orders n ≥ 1.

items.q: Do all wavelengths give grating maxima at the same angles?
items.correct: No. sin θ = nλ/d, so each wavelength has its own set of angles; only the central maximum is common to all.
items.misconception: The positions of the maxima, and the number of orders, are fixed by the grating alone, so every wavelength gives maxima in the same places.
items.why: Most practical work uses a single wavelength, so the pattern seems to be a property of the grating, like the lines ruled on it. Replace a red laser with a green one and the maxima move inwards. The grating fixes d; the wavelength fixes where the maxima fall.
